title: Find the Maximum Length of Valid Subsequence II
statement:
Take a subsequence `sub` of the integer array `nums` (some elements kept in their original order, the rest deleted). Call it **valid** when every two neighbouring elements of `sub` add up to the same remainder modulo the positive integer `k`; for a subsequence of length `x` that means

`(sub[0] + sub[1]) % k == (sub[1] + sub[2]) % k == ... == (sub[x - 2] + sub[x - 1]) % k`.

Find how many elements the longest valid subsequence of `nums` has, and return that count.
notes:
## Intuition

If `(a + b) % k == (b + c) % k`, then `a` and `c` leave the same remainder. So in a valid subsequence the elements at even positions all share one remainder and the elements at odd positions share another (possibly the same one), and any subsequence whose remainders alternate like that is valid. Only remainders matter, which suggests a table indexed by two remainders: the remainder of the last element and the remainder it alternates with. Checking every pair-sum remainder with an O(n²) chain search per remainder also works, but costs O(k·n²).

## Approach

1. Make a `k` by `k` table `dp` of zeros. `dp[last][prev]` is the length of the longest subsequence seen so far that ends with remainder `last` and alternates with remainder `prev` (the element before the end, if any, has remainder `prev`).
2. For each `num`, compute `last = num % k`.
3. For every remainder `prev`, the best subsequence this element can extend ends with `prev` and alternates with `last`, which is `dp[prev][last]`. Appending `num` gives `dp[last][prev] = dp[prev][last] + 1`.
4. Track the largest value written in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`k = 2`, so the remainders of `[1,2,3,4,5]` are `1,0,1,0,1`.
- `num = 1`: `dp[1][0] = 1`, `dp[1][1] = 1`.
- `num = 2`: `dp[0][0] = 1`, `dp[0][1] = dp[1][0] + 1 = 2`.
- `num = 3`: `dp[1][0] = dp[0][1] + 1 = 3`, `dp[1][1] = 2`.
- `num = 4`: `dp[0][0] = 2`, `dp[0][1] = dp[1][0] + 1 = 4`.
- `num = 5`: `dp[1][0] = dp[0][1] + 1 = 5`, `dp[1][1] = 3`.

`best = 5`: the whole array alternates between odd and even.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k² + n·k): building the table, then `k` updates per element.
- Space: O(k²) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- Read the mirrored cell `dp[prev][last]`: the new element extends a subsequence that ends with `prev`, not one that ends with `last`.
- `prev === last` is allowed (all elements with one remainder); the statement reads the cell before writing it, so this case works too.
- It is a subsequence, not a subarray: elements may be skipped, so never reset the table between elements.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[last][prev]` | longest subsequence so far ending with remainder `last` and alternating with remainder `prev` |
| `best` | longest valid subsequence found so far |
| `num` | the element being appended |
| `last` | `num % k`, the remainder of that element |
| `prev` | the remainder of the element just before it |

narration.2: A k by k table: dp[last][prev] is the longest subsequence ending with remainder last that alternates with remainder prev.
narration.3: No subsequence has been built yet.
narration.5: Consider the elements in their original order, as a subsequence must.
narration.6: Only the remainder of the element matters for validity.
narration.7: Try every remainder that the element before this one could have.
narration.8: Extend the best subsequence ending with prev that alternates with last; it now ends with last.
narration.9: Remember the longest subsequence seen so far.
narration.12: best is the length of the longest valid subsequence.
